Notion: https://app.notion.com/p/Element-Interactivity-Management-Decouple-Interconnected-Decisions-69fa9aed534483b8b01f019158427381

## UX-456 — Cognitive Tunneling Defense: Protect Critical Info in Stressed Users
- Score 2 · Cognitive Load / Attention Management
- Tags: cognitive-load, decision-making
- Goals: Reduce Cognitive Load
- Use when: Essential for any dashboard, monitoring, or control interface used under time pressure, during incidents, or by users who are cognitively multitasking.

**Why.** Cognitive tunneling (also called 'tunnel vision') occurs when users under high cognitive load narrow their attentional field to the most immediately salient task, becoming effectively blind to important peripheral information. This is particularly dangerous in dashboards and control-panel UIs, where critical alerts may sit outside the user's focal zone during high-pressure moments. Dashboard design must assume that the most critical information will be needed precisely when users are most cognitively loaded.

**Do.**
- Place highest-priority alerts and KPIs in the primary focal zone (top-center or top-left) for dashboards — not in sidebars or footers.
- Design a clear visual hierarchy of alert severities (critical, warning, info) so that even a cursory glance surface the most urgent items first.
- Limit dashboard information density; when a user is under load, they can only meaningfully process the top 3–5 data points — design for that reality, not for the all-data scenario.
- Use contrast, size, and motion hierarchy: critical elements should be visually largest and highest-contrast; supporting data should be visually quieter.
- In time-critical interfaces (incident management, trading, emergency dispatch), implement 'focus mode' that auto-filters to the most critical items and hides routine data.
- Use redundant coding (color + icon + label + position) for any critical state, since the user under load may only process one channel.

**Measure.** Effectiveness: Task success rate, Error rate; Efficiency: Time on task; Satisfaction & Perception: Confidence rating, Ease-of-use score; How to measure: Conduct usability tests simulating high-stress or high-stakes scenarios and measure error rate and task success rate; compare critical-information noticeability between layouts designed with and without cognitive-tunneling defenses.

Sources: [Design Principles: Hick's Law — Marvel Blog](https://marvelapp.com/blog/design-principles-hicks-law%E2%80%8A-%E2%80%8Aquick-decision-making/) · [CASTLE Framework for Workplace Applications UX — Nielsen Norman Group](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/castle-framework/) · [Selective Attention & Content Blindness — UX Knowledge Base](https://uxknowledgebase.com/selective-attention-content-blindness-in-ux-design-e53033b597c6)
Wireframe: https://files.catbox.moe/lgkm6x.jpg
Notion: https://app.notion.com/p/Cognitive-Tunneling-Defense-Protect-Critical-Info-in-Stressed-Users-c22a9aed5344839c804d014ac7f32570

## UX-460 — Modality Effect: Pair Visual Content With Audio Narration for Complex Instructions
- Score 2 · Cognitive Load / Multimodal Design
- Tags: accessibility, cognitive-load
- Goals: Improve Readability & Visual Clarity; Reduce Cognitive Load
- Use when: Most valuable for tutorials, onboarding flows, step-by-step instructional content, and complex process explanations — especially for first-time users and system-paced experiences.

**Why.** The modality effect, established by Sweller and Mayer, shows that combining visual graphics with spoken narration is more effective than combining graphics with on-screen text. When both text and graphics occupy the visual channel, they compete for the same working memory resource. Distributing explanatory content across visual (diagram) and auditory (narration) channels uses both of Baddeley's working memory subsystems simultaneously, effectively doubling the available processing capacity for complex content.

**Do.**
- For product tours, onboarding flows, and tutorials involving diagrams or process visualizations, pair the visual with spoken narration rather than on-screen text blocks.
- In instructional videos or animated walkthroughs, use voiceover to explain what is being shown rather than overlaying text on the animation.
- When on-screen text is necessary alongside visual content, keep it minimal (labels, key terms only) — do not replicate the full narration as text on the same screen.
- Use the modality principle selectively: for self-paced reference content that users will re-consult, written text plus visuals may be preferable since users can re-read at their own pace.
- For complex configuration screens or setup wizards, consider offering a 'guided mode' that uses audio prompts alongside the visual UI.
- Respect accessibility: always provide captions and transcripts for audio content, and ensure the visual-only path is equally complete.

**Measure.** Effectiveness: Completion rate, Error rate; Efficiency: Time on task, Training time; Satisfaction & Perception: Ease-of-use score, Confidence rating; How to measure: Compare task completion rate and error counts in usability tests between visual-only instructions and visual-plus-audio paired formats; measure training time reduction for onboarding flows that adopt the modality approach.

Sources: [The Modality Effect in Multimedia Instructions — Edinburgh](https://conferences.inf.ed.ac.uk/cogsci2001/pdf-files/1024.pdf) · [The Modality Effect: How to Maximize Learning — Mind My Learning](https://mindmylearning.com/blog/modality-effect-maximize-learning/) · [Mayer's 12 Principles of Multimedia Learning — Digital Learning Institute](https://www.digitallearninginstitute.com/blog/mayers-principles-multimedia-learning)

## UX-473 — Germane Load Support: Design for Schema Building in Learning Interfaces
- Score 2 · Cognitive Load / Learning and Onboarding
- Tags: cognitive-load
- Goals: Reduce Learning Curve for Complex Tools; Reduce Cognitive Load
- Use when: Apply to onboarding flows, feature education, in-product tutorials, and any interface where users need to build durable skill rather than just complete a one-time task.

**Why.** Germane cognitive load refers to the working memory resources devoted to schema construction — building long-term knowledge structures that permanently reduce future intrinsic load. Unlike extraneous load (always bad) and intrinsic load (inherent to task complexity), germane load represents productive cognitive investment. UI designers can support germane load by structuring onboarding and learning interactions to facilitate schema building, using spaced repetition, worked examples, and deliberate practice patterns.

**Do.**
- Structure onboarding to teach conceptual models, not just button locations: users who understand why a feature works will generalize to related features with less assistance.
- Use worked examples in feature introductions: show a completed, annotated example before asking users to perform the task independently.
- Design interactive tutorials that require users to perform actions themselves (not just watch), as self-generation aids schema encoding.
- Introduce features in an order that builds conceptual schema cumulatively: teach foundational concepts before dependent features, not alphabetically or by complexity.
- Implement spaced re-exposure for complex features: a brief contextual reminder on the 2nd and 5th use is more effective than a comprehensive tutorial on first use.
- In help documentation, organize content by user goal and mental model, not by feature or technical category — this matches how users retrieve knowledge from schemas.

**Measure.** Effectiveness: Task success rate, Completion rate; Efficiency: Training time, Time on task; Satisfaction & Perception: Ease-of-use score, Confidence rating; How to measure: Measure training time and task success rate in learning sessions with and without schema-building scaffolds; use pre/post knowledge assessments to quantify schema acquisition gains alongside usability metrics.

Sources: [Cognitive Load Theory and Instructional Design — University of Kentucky](https://www.uky.edu/~gmswan3/544/Cognitive_Load_&_ID.pdf) · [The Expertise Reversal Effect — The eLearning Coach](https://theelearningcoach.com/learning/novice-versus-expert-design-strategies/) · [Cognitive Load Theory — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cognitive_load)
Wireframe: https://files.catbox.moe/8qx743.jpg
Notion: https://app.notion.com/p/Germane-Load-Support-Design-for-Schema-Building-in-Learning-Interfaces-703a9aed534483e99a45012ea31f473f
